Ametryn (Ref: G 34162 )
Last updated: 11/06/2026
(Also known as: ametryne; ametrex)
SUMMARY
Ametyn is a triazine herbicide. It is moderately soluble in water but much more so in organic solvents. It is quite volatile and not expected to leach to groundwater. It is moderately persistent in soils and can persist for a long time in water under certain conditions. It is moderately toxic to mammals and a recognised irritant. Ametryn is moderately toxic to most aquatic organisms, honeybees and earthworms but less so to birds.
Hazard alerts

The following Pesticide Hazard Tricolour (PHT) alerts are based on the data in the tables below. An absence of an alert does not imply the substance has no implications for human health, biodiversity or the environment but just that we do not have the data to form a judgement. The alerts for Highly Hazardous Pesticides (HHPs) are based on applying the FAO/WHO (Type 1) and the PAN (Type II) criteria to PPDB data. Further details on the HHP indicators are given in the tables below. Neither the PHT nor the HHP hazard alerts take account of usage patterns or exposure, thus they do not represent risk.

Formulation and application details
Available in a range of formulations including emulsifiable concentrates, flowable concentrates and wettable powders.
Commercial production
The production of ametryn involves a multi-step chemical synthesis process typically using microchannel reactor technology for efficiency and precision. Initially, atrazine solution, alkali liquor, and sodium methyl mercaptide are fed into a microchannel reactor where they react to form an intermediate compound. This mixture is then separated in a layering device, and the upper layer is reacted with sodium hypochlorite in a second microchannel reactor. After another separation step, the oil phase is transferred to a distillation kettle to remove solvents. The desolventised material is cooled and crystallized to yield the final ametryn product.
Impact on climate of production and use
Data for the amount of life cycle GHGs produced by ametryn are not available in the public domain. However, whilst estimates vary, more general data suggests that between 18 and 27 kilograms of CO₂e is emitted per kilogram of herbicide produced.
